3. It is the case of the plaintiff that they sent biris of their manufacture by train to M. Kudratullah of Saidpur, District Rangpur under Railway Receipt No. AO50061 dated 24.10.51 and forwarded the railway Receipt through the Central Bank of India Ltd. Calcutta for realization of the price of the biris through its Rangpur branch office. The biris reached its destination, but the Sub-divisional Officer, Nilphamari by his order wrongfully and illegally withheld the biris and subsequently the said Sub-Divisional Officer permitted the consignee M. Kudrutullah to take delivery of the biris on payment of the value of the said railway Receipt in Pakistan currency. The said M. Kudrutullah deposited Tk. 10,230-11-6 on 15.11.51 in the Central Bank of India Ltd., Rangpur branch. The said amount was attached by the said Sub- Divisional Officer for the realization of demands in Certificate case No 45 and 46 (misc) of 1949-50, stated against M/s. Khorabhoy Jagmal and others. Subsequent thereto the said Sub-Divisional Officer, Nilphamari compelled the Central Bank of India Ltd., Rangpur branch to pay a sum of Tk. 10,197/5/ to him out of the attached money in the hands of the said Bank. The bank accordingly paid this amount demanded, under Bank Draft No. 02639/1 dated 161-53 which was encashed by the Sub-Divisional Officer, Nilphamari on 28.1.52. The said sum was attached towards the liquidation of the demands in Certificate case Nos. 45 and 46 (misc.) of 1949-50 by an order of the said Sub- Divisional Officer on 15.5.52 against M/s. Khorabhoy Jagmall and others in respect of debt due to the certificate holder. Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Dacca. Thus according to the plaintiff, this was wrongful and illegal appropriation of money belonging to the plaintiff Company for the liquidation of the certificate debt for which the plaintiff, company was not liable. The plaintiff company applied for refund of the said amount, but the prayer was refused which has caused a loss to the plaintiff company to the extent of Tk. 10 197/5/- by way of compensation for illegal and wrongful taking of the said money together with charges amounting to Tk. 802/11 /- The total claim thus was laid at Tk. 11.000/-. 

 4. The defendant, erstwhile Government of East Bengal filed a written statement and contested the suit. The case of the defendant was that Khorabhoy Jagmall and others carried on a partnership business in Biris at Syedpur. A sum of Tk. 21,000/- was due from partnership business to the Government on account of commercial tax and for the realization of the said amount certificate case Nos. 45 and 46 of 1949 50 were started against the said partnership firm of Khorabhoy Jagmall. After the cases were started the said Khorabhoy Jagmall in order to defraud the Government started a firm under the name and style of Lucky Biri Company in the names of his sons Deyaram Deoji and Wallamji Khorabhoy and employees Karman Narain and Wallamji Deoji with its head office at Calcutta. Khorabhoy Jagmall supplied the capital of the firm. The fact, of the attachment has not been denied in the written statement, but it has been stated in the said written statement that the, realization was done duly and legally. 

 6. Mr. Sultan Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing in support of the appeal has canvassed before us firstly that (1) in the facts and circumstances of the case the Court below erred in law and fact in not holding that the deed of partnership is nothing but a creation of a firm for evading payment of taxes due from Khorabhoy Jagmall, (2) Income tax assessment order Exts. 2 and 3 wrongly considered by the Court below as evidence to show that there was no joint family with Khorabhoy Jagmall (3) that the Court below erred in law and fact in not holding in the facts and circumstances of the case that the plaintiff firm is liable for the legal dues of Khorabhoy Jagmall (4) that the Court below ought to have evidence considered the adduced on behalf of the plaintiff keeping an eve on the fact that the firm was created to avoid the legal claim of the defendant, and lastly, that on the facts and circumstances of the case and after correctly approaching the evidence on record the Court below ought to have held that the plaintiff company was started with the capital of Khorabhoy Jagmall. In support of his contentions the learned Deputy Attorney General has placed his reliance on the theory of Lifting the Veil and referred to the Principle of Modern Company Law, 3rd Edition by L.C.B. Gower page 189. The relevant passage is at pages 210 and 211. The decision in the case of Gilford Motor Co. Vs. Horne reported in Law Report (1933) 1 Ch. Division page 935 and P.L.D. 1971 (S.C.) 585. 

 7. The plaintiff has examined five witnesses and the defendant examined one. A number of exhibits have been filed on behalf of the plaintiff in support of their case. 

 10. P.W. 5 Anil Kumar Sarkar is a formal witness. D.W.1 Bharat Chandra Adhikary is a clerk who has spoken about Khorabhoy's family had a partnership business at Syedpur and a sum of Tk. 21,000/- was due from the partnership business to the Government on account of Commercial Tax, for the realization of which Certificate Case No. 45 and 46 of 1949 50 were started against the firm. He has further stated that to defraud the Government Khorabhoy Jagmal started a fictitious firm under the name and style of Lucky Biri Co., with bead office in Calcutta. In cross-examination, however, this D.W. 1 failed to give the names of other certificate debtors and be also failed to give the names of the employees of Khorabhai. 

 “It will therefore be seen that in a number of important respects the legislature has rent the veil woven by the Solomon case. Particularly is this so in the sphere of taxation and in the steps which have been taken towards the recognition of enterprise-entity rather than corporation entity. The Courts, however, have only construed statutes as "cracking open the corporate shell" when compelled to do so by clear words of the statute; indeed they have gone out of their way to avoid this construction whenever possible.” 

 The author at page 210 writes, "We now turn to a number of isolated illustrations of circumstances in which the Courts have felt themselves free to disregard the corporate entity. The first of these is where there is "fraud or improper conduct". In reaching the conclusion after elaborate discussion of various decisions the author has found that the Courts are in general precluded by Solomon's case from treating a company as the "alias, agent, trustee of nominee" of its members. They will nevertheless do so if corporate personality being blatantly used as cloak for fraud or improper conduct. In the opinion of tile author the Courts have found it essential to the lift the veil for certain purposes owing to the fact that a company is only an artificial person. In the case of Gilford Motor Co. vs. Horne upon which reliance has been placed by the learned Deputy Attorney General it is found that the Court of Appeal has also held "I am quite satisfied that this company was formed as a device, a stratagem, in order to mask the effective carrying-on of a business as of Mr. E.B. Horne". At page 961 following a decision by Lindley L.J. in the case of Smith vs. Hancock reported in (1) 1894/2 Ch page 377 and 385 held, "if the evidence admitted of the conclusion that what was being done was a mere cloak or sham, and that in truth the business was being earned on by the wife and Kerr for the defendant, or by the defendant through his wife for Kerr, I certainly should not hesitate to draw that con- elusion, and to grant the plaintiff relief accordingly." Upon this a conclusion was drawn by the noble lord of the Court of Appeal in the following terms: "I hold that company was a mere cloak or sham." The same view was taken of the matter in this decision by Lord Haworth, Master of the Rolls and also by Romer lord justice in allowing the appeal. It was observed "as I think he did conclude, that this defendant company was formed and was carrying on business merely as cloak or sham for the purpose of enabling the defendant Home to commit the breach of the convenant that he entered into deliberately with the plaintiffs on the occasion of and as consideration for his employment as managing director," Chief Justice Hamoodur Rahman in the decision in the case of the President Vs. Mr. Justice Shaukat Ali reported in PLD 1971 (SC) 585 relevant page at 617 accepted, this principle of lifting the veil and on reference to L.C.B. Gower's Modern Company Law, 3rd Edition page 183 to 209 and also Willian Cory & Son Limited Vs. Darman Long & company Limited 1936(1) All. E.R. 386 held: 

 “The trend of decisions since the above enunciation of the law in Solomon's case appears, however, to show that in a number of important respects both the Courts and the Legislatures have rent the veil which was recognized in the above-mentioned decision to be almost inviolable. The growing tendency appears to be rather to look at the substance and not to allow the vision to be clouded by the shadow of the corporate personality. Thus where the corporate personality is being used merely as a cloak for fraud or improper conduct or where it can be established that the corporate personality is merely acting as an agent or trustee for someone else, be he an individual or another subsidiary company or where it is necessary to determine the true character of the corporate personality for other purposes, such as to determine its tax liability or its quasi criminal liability or as to whether the corporate body is an enemy concern or not, or a mere trustee for certain purposes, the Courts have not hesitated to look behind the veil of incorporation. 

 Whatever might be the position of third parties, vis-a-vis the company and the liabilities of its share-holders, it does appear that there is no bar to the Courts lifting the veil of incorporation to determine the true relationship of the shareholders with regard to their dealings with the company or to ascertain the true nature of the company itself in matters which are governed by other statutes or where other considerations necessitate the taking of such a step In the present case too, we are not concerned with the liability of the respondent as a member of the companies but we are concerned, in terms of a Code of Conduct drawn up under the constitution, with determining as a matter of public policy as to whether the association of a Judge of a Superior Court with such concerns constitutes involvement in activities of trade, business or industry. For this purpose we think we are entitled to go behind the shadow of incorporation in order to ascertain as to what the real nature of the association of the respondent was with these concerns.” 

 13. The decisions and passages referred to of the Text Book of L.C.B. Gower though confined to the Companies registered under the Companies Act we think that the principle involved there is equally available in the case of partnership which are registered under the Partnership Act. In application of the said principle we find in this case that the plaintiff company was formed only at a point of time when tax and liabilities of the other company of Khorabhai Jagmal came to be assessed by the Taxing Authority of the erstwhile Province of East Bengal. The plaintiff company stepped into the shoes of the business of the company that was closed down since the time of its information of the tax liabilities as is available from the evidence of the plaintiff's witnesses. 

 14. In this view of the matter, we think that the learned Subordinate Judge had wrongly kept the legal entity of the plaintiff company distinct and separate from the other company of Khorabhai Jagmal. There is no doubt that there is absence of evidence from the defendant's side as regards the persons against whom the certificate case was started besides Khorabhai Jagmal but taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case we conclude that the plaintiff company is nothing but a sham one and a cloak used by Khorabhai Jagmal to evade the taxes imposed upon it by the taxing authority of the erstwhile Province of East Bengal.
